body.script: Welcome, everyone, to Harbour Bike Tours. I'm Marcus, and I'll be your guide this afternoon. The tour lasts about three hours and covers roughly twenty kilometres, so it's a fairly gentle ride, but there are a couple of hills near the old fort. We set off from the front of the ferry terminal at two o'clock sharp. Actually, I should say two fifteen today, because the bikes were delivered late. Please be at the meeting point ten minutes before that. You'll each be given a helmet, and these are compulsory, I'm afraid. You'll also find a small repair kit under every seat. If anything goes wrong with your bike, don't try to fix it yourself. Just call me on the number printed on your map. Our first stop will be the fish market, where you'll have fifteen minutes to buy a snack. Then we ride along the river to the botanical gardens, which is the best place for photographs. We'll stop for a proper break at a cafe beside the lake at around four o'clock, and the tour finishes back at the ferry terminal at about five thirty. The price includes the bike hire, the helmet and one drink at the cafe, but not the entrance fee for the gardens, which is six pounds fifty. If you'd like to pay by card rather than cash, please do that before we leave, because there are no machines on the route. Finally, if it rains, the tour will still go ahead unless the wind is very strong, in which case we'll rearrange it for the following day.

body.script: Today I'd like to look at the role of green space in cities, and in particular at three benefits that planners often cite. The first is temperature. On a hot day, a city centre can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, because buildings and roads absorb heat. Trees help by providing shade, but also, and this is less obvious, by releasing water vapour, which cools the air around them. In one study, areas with at least thirty per cent tree cover were consistently cooler than those with less than ten. The second benefit is mental health. Several surveys have found that residents who live within five hundred metres of a park report lower levels of stress. Interestingly, the size of the park matters less than you might expect. What seems to count is that people can reach it easily and feel safe there. The third benefit is biodiversity. Even small green areas, such as roadside verges or roof gardens, can support insects and birds, provided they are planted with native species. Now, you might assume that more green space is always better, but there are trade-offs. Land in city centres is extremely expensive, and every hectare turned into a park is a hectare that cannot be used for housing. Some planners have therefore turned to what they call green corridors, narrow strips of planting that link existing parks. These cost less, but critics argue that they are too narrow to offer real benefits to wildlife. For your assignment, I'd like you to choose one European city and evaluate its green space policy against these three benefits. You should aim for around two thousand words, and the deadline is the twelfth of March.

body.script: Hello, this is a message for Ms Rivera from Brightwater Language School. My name is Daniel Okafor, and I'm calling about your enrolment on the evening English course. Unfortunately, the class that you chose for Tuesdays has been cancelled because we didn't have enough students. I can offer you a place in the Thursday class instead, which runs from six thirty to eight thirty, starting on the ninth of October. The course lasts ten weeks and the fee is four hundred and eighty pounds, payable by the end of this month. If you're not able to attend on Thursdays, we do have a Saturday morning class beginning at nine fifteen, but that one is slightly more expensive, at five hundred and twenty pounds. You'll need to bring your passport on the first day so we can make a copy for our records, and a notebook, as we don't provide those. Please call me back before Friday on the number you were given when you enrolled. Thank you, and I hope to see you soon.
